items.title: Google Patches Actively Exploited Chrome V8 Zero-Day CVE-2026-85046 (CVSS 8.8)
items.summary: A type confusion bug in Chrome's V8 JavaScript/WebAssembly engine allows arbitrary code execution inside the browser sandbox via a crafted webpage. Patched September 3 in Chrome 152.0.7977.82/83. Discovered by researcher Serotav on August 4. This is the sixth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, alongside CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, and CVE-2026-11645.
items.why: No user interaction beyond visiting a malicious or compromised page is required. Exploitation is confirmed in the wild. Any unpatched Chrome user is at risk via phishing links, malvertising, or watering-hole attacks. Update Chrome to 152.0.7977.82 or later immediately.

items.title: SonicWall SMA1000 Zero-Days CVE-2026-83548 (CVSS 10.0) + CVE-2026-83549 Chained for Unauthenticated RCE — CISA KEV
items.summary: CVE-2026-83548 is a pre-auth SSRF (CVSS 10.0) in the SMA1000 Workplace interface that enables an unauthenticated attacker to pivot through the appliance to sensitive internal services. Chained with CVE-2026-83549 (OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console), it achieves full unauthenticated RCE. SonicWall confirmed active exploitation. Both added to the CISA KEV catalog on September 2, 2026.
items.why: SMA1000 appliances sit at the network edge as SSL VPN gateways — compromise grants attackers a foothold into enterprise networks with zero credentials required. CISA mandated federal civilian agency remediation by September 5, 2026. Any internet-exposed SMA1000 should be patched or taken offline immediately.

items.title: Iran-Nexus APT 'Screening Serpens' Escalates Espionage Operations Across Five Countries Since February 2026 Conflict
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracked Screening Serpens, a prolific Iranian APT group identified as among the most active in 2026 by Group-IB. The group significantly ramped up operations following the regional conflict that began in February 2026, deploying two distinct RAT variant families against entities across at least five countries to conduct credential harvesting and intelligence collection.
items.why: This demonstrates how geopolitical conflict directly and immediately accelerates nation-state cyber operations. The dual-RAT deployment suggests coordinated, parallel intelligence-gathering campaigns across multiple sectors. Defenders in the Middle East and allied nations should review exposure, rotate credentials, and monitor for spear-phishing lures referencing the ongoing conflict.

items.title: Critical Gitea RCE CVE-2026-60004 (CVSS 9.8) Actively Exploited to Deploy Miner-Like Payloads — CISA KEV
items.summary: A Git hook injection flaw in Gitea allows any user with repository write access to execute arbitrary OS commands as the Gitea service account via the diffpatch API. On open-registration instances (the default Gitea setting), an attacker can register an account and immediately exploit the chain. Affects all versions from 1.17; patched in Gitea 1.27.1. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on August 25 with a federal remediation deadline of August 28.
items.why: Gitea is widely self-hosted in enterprise DevSecOps pipelines and source code environments. The near-zero exploitation bar — any authenticated user on open-registration instances — combined with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation makes this critical. Attackers are deploying cryptominers and likely establishing persistence for supply-chain attacks. Patch to 1.27.1 and disable open registration.

items.title: ClickFix, FileFix & ConsentFix: Novel Human-Layer Attack Chains Bypass EDR and MFA Without Deploying Malware
items.summary: Researchers documented three related attack chains — ClickFix (luring victims into pasting malicious clipboard commands into Run dialogs), FileFix (fake file-open prompts executing hidden commands), and ConsentFix (spoofed OAuth consent screens stealing session tokens) — that trick users into bypassing endpoint detection, MFA, and other security controls by completing apparently legitimate actions. CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report noted 82% of detections were entirely malware-free, reinforcing this trend.
items.why: These techniques are malware-free and exploit human trust rather than software flaws, making them invisible to most EDR and AV solutions. ConsentFix in particular abuses legitimate OAuth flows to steal tokens, fully defeating MFA. Organizations need phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/FIDO2 hardware keys), strict OAuth application allow-listing, and targeted user awareness training for these specific lure patterns.
items.source: Infosecurity Magazine / CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report
